questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. The ulcer has clean, indurated edges and a non-purulent base. Regional lymph nodes are rubbery and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy of the serous exudate would most likely show:
questions.exp: The painless, indurated chancre with non-tender lymphadenopathy is the classic presentation of primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy reveals motile spirochetes with characteristic corkscrew motility.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with multiple painful, soft ulcers on the prepuce with undermined edges, and ipsilateral painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. The causative organism is best identified by:
opts: Gram stain showing gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish' pattern
Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi presents with painful soft ulcers with undermined edges and painful inguinal bubo. Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli in a 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern.

questions.q: A 45-year-old leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops sudden onset erythema, warmth, and tenderness of pre-existing skin lesions along with fever and malaise. Nerve function remains unchanged. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: Continue MDT and add clofazimine at higher dose
questions.exp: This is a Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction). MDT should never be stopped. Prednisolone is the drug of choice. Clofazimine at higher dose is used for Type 2 (ENL) reactions, not Type 1.

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy develops painful nodular erythematous lesions on the face and extremities, fever, iritis, and orchitis. The Mitsuda reaction in this patient would most likely be:
questions.exp: This presentation describes Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) / Type 2 lepra reaction, which occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. In lepromatous leprosy, the Mitsuda (lepromin) reaction is negative due to specific anergy to M. leprae.

questions.q: A 25-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the right T5 dermatome, with burning pain preceding the rash by 2 days. The most common serious complication to watch for in this age group is:
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common complication of herpes zoster. Although more common and severe in the elderly (>60 years), it can occur in younger patients. In younger immunocompetent patients, the risk is lower but PHN remains the most frequent serious complication.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the mouth and nose. Culture grows beta-hemolytic streptococci. The most feared systemic complication of this infection is:
questions.exp: Impetigo due to Group A Streptococcus (nephritogenic strains) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Unlike pharyngeal streptococcal infection, skin streptococcal infection does NOT cause rheumatic fever.

questions.q: A 40-year-old diabetic presents with rapidly spreading redness, warmth, and swelling of the lower leg with systemic toxicity, bullae, and crepitus. The most appropriate initial management is:
opts: Emergency surgical debridement with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Crepitus (gas in tissues), bullae, and systemic toxicity are hallmarks. The mainstay of treatment is emergency surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Delay in surgery significantly increases mortality.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female presents with well-demarcated hypopigmented macules on the face and trunk that fluoresce yellow-green under Wood's lamp. KOH examination shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum orbiculare). KOH shows short hyphae and spores in 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. Under Wood's lamp, it shows yellow-green fluorescence.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient with CD4 count of 80 cells/uL presents with extensive verrucous plaques on the hands and feet with thick subungual debris. KOH examination shows numerous scabies mites, eggs, and fecal pellets. This condition is best described as:
questions.exp: Norwegian (crusted) scabies occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant recipients, elderly in institutions). It is characterized by thousands to millions of mites (vs. ~15 in classic scabies), hyperkeratotic/crusted plaques, and is highly contagious but often not pruritic.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on the trunk and flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear deposits of IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen is most likely:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin in elderly patients. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at DEJ (roof of blister on salt-split skin). Autoantibodies target BP180 (BPAG2/Collagen XVII) and BP230 (BPAG1).

questions.q: A 50-year-old female presents with flaccid bullae and erosions in the oral cavity for 3 months, followed by involvement of the trunk. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Histopathology shows suprabasal acantholysis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris presents with flaccid bullae and oral erosions (mucous membrane involvement), positive Nikolsky sign, and suprabasal acantholysis on histology. The target antigen is Desmoglein 3 (with or without Desmoglein 1). Pemphigus foliaceus does NOT involve mucous membranes.

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient presents with intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at the dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is strongly associated with celiac disease/gluten sensitivity. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillae. Treatment is dapsone for rapid symptom relief and gluten-free diet as long-term management. Dapsone does not affect the underlying enteropathy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). The most specific antibody for this diagnosis that also correlates with disease activity (especially nephritis) is:
questions.exp: In SLE, anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific (>99%) and correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. Anti-Sm is highly specific but does not correlate with activity. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female presents with progressive skin tightening of the fingers and face, Raynaud's phenomenon, and dysphagia. She has telangiectasias and calcinosis. The antibody most likely to be positive is:
questions.exp: The CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is associated with anti-centromere antibody. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and is a risk factor for pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female presents with heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, periungual erythema, and proximal muscle weakness. Muscle enzymes are elevated. This condition is most strongly associated with an underlying malignancy in which age group?
opts: No association with malignancy at any age
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults over 40 years is associated with internal malignancy (15-25% of cases), most commonly ovarian, lung, GI, and breast cancers. Juvenile dermatomyositis (in children) is NOT associated with malignancy. All adult DM patients require thorough malignancy workup.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a pearly, telangiectatic nodule on the nose that has been slowly growing for 2 years. Biopsy shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and artifactual clefting. The most appropriate primary treatment is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma on the nose (H-zone of the face) is a high-risk location requiring Mohs micrographic surgery for highest cure rate (>99%) with maximum tissue conservation. Mohs is the treatment of choice for BCC at critical cosmetic/functional areas, recurrent BCC, and morpheaform BCC.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male farmer presents with a non-healing ulcer on his lower lip with indurated, everted edges and regional lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows keratin pearls and individual cell keratinization. The most important prognostic factor is:
questions.exp: In squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the presence of lymph node metastasis is the single most important prognostic factor for survival. Regional lymph node involvement significantly worsens the prognosis. The lip is a common site for SCC in farmers/outdoor workers due to UV exposure.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with an irregular, asymmetric pigmented lesion on his back, 12mm diameter, with variegated colors including black, brown, and pink areas, and an irregular border. Dermoscopy reveals atypical pigment network and irregular streaks. The recommended initial diagnostic procedure is:
opts: Incisional biopsy of the most pigmented area
questions.exp: For suspected melanoma, excisional biopsy with narrow margins (1-2mm) is the recommended initial diagnostic procedure. This allows accurate Breslow thickness measurement (most important prognostic factor). Shave biopsy is contraindicated as it prevents accurate depth measurement. Incisional biopsy is acceptable for large lesions only.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the elbows and scalp, nail pitting, and salmon patch. Auspitz sign is positive. Which nail feature would most suggest concomitant psoriatic arthritis?
questions.exp: Nail changes in psoriasis, particularly onycholysis (oil-drop sign), subungual hyperkeratosis, and nail dystrophy, are the strongest predictors of psoriatic arthritis (PsA). The prevalence of PsA in patients with nail psoriasis is significantly higher than those without nail involvement.

questions.q: A 10-year-old atopic child presents with flexural dermatitis, xerosis, and lichenification of antecubital and popliteal fossae. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Which of the following features is NOT a minor criterion of atopic dermatitis (Hanifin and Rajka criteria)?
questions.exp: Photosensitivity is NOT a recognized minor criterion of atopic dermatitis per Hanifin and Rajka criteria. Minor criteria include: xerosis, ichthyosis, keratosis pilaris, immediate skin test reactivity, elevated IgE, Dennie-Morgan folds, pityriasis alba, nipple eczema, white dermographism, food intolerance, environmental/emotional influences, and others.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female presents with depigmented macules and patches on the face and dorsum of hands since 5 years. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. The dermoscopic finding that best predicts a positive response to repigmentation therapy is:
questions.exp: Perifollicular pigmentation seen on dermoscopy in vitiligo indicates preserved melanocyte reservoirs in hair follicles. These follicular melanocytes are the source of repigmentation during treatment, and their presence is a positive prognostic marker. Leukotrichia (white hair) indicates loss of follicular melanocytes and predicts poor treatment response.

questions.q: A 40-year-old patient is prescribed isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to isotretinoin?
opts: Elevated liver enzymes (2x upper limit of normal)
questions.exp: Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication to isotretinoin due to its severe teratogenicity (retinoic acid embryopathy). It can cause CNS, cardiovascular, craniofacial, and thymic malformations. Mildly elevated triglycerides and liver enzymes are relative contraindications requiring monitoring.

questions.q: A patient on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops sudden onset pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. The most likely underlying predisposing factor is:
questions.exp: Dapsone can cause dose-dependent hemolytic anemia in all patients, but severe hemolysis occurs in patients with G6PD deficiency. Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) and bite cells on peripheral smear are characteristic of G6PD deficiency. G6PD levels should be checked before starting dapsone.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents for laser hair removal of the upper lip. She has Fitzpatrick skin type IV. The safest and most effective laser for her is:
questions.exp: Nd:YAG laser (1064nm) is the safest choice for darker skin types (Fitzpatrick IV-VI). Its longer wavelength passes through melanin-rich epidermis with less epidermal absorption, reducing the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and burns. Alexandrite and Ruby lasers have higher epidermal melanin absorption, making them riskier in darker skin types.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with deep-set hyperpigmented atrophic scars on the cheeks following severe acne. The most appropriate treatment specifically for ice-pick scars is:
questions.exp: Ice-pick scars are narrow, deep, sharp-bordered scars that require punch excision or punch elevation. They extend deep into the dermis/subcutis and cannot be adequately treated by surface resurfacing techniques. After punch excision, the small wound heals with a flat scar that can then be resurfaced. Fractional CO2 is better for rolling/boxcar scars.

questions.q: A 28-year-old presents with erythematous, greasy, scaling patches on the nasolabial folds, eyebrows, and scalp. KOH examination is negative. The most likely pathophysiology involves:
questions.exp: Seborrheic dermatitis is caused by an inflammatory reaction to Malassezia species (M. globosa, M. restricta) present in sebum-rich areas. The pathogenesis involves Malassezia lipase activity producing oleic acid and arachidonic acid metabolites, triggering skin barrier disruption and Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. KOH is negative as Malassezia is a commensal.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with lymphedema of the right leg for 10 years and now develops multiple reddish-purple nodules on the edematous skin. Biopsy shows irregular vascular spaces lined by atypical endothelial cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Stewart-Treves syndrome is a rare but aggressive angiosarcoma arising in the setting of chronic lymphedema, classically described after mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, but can occur with any chronic lymphedema. It has a very poor prognosis. Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8 associated and typically seen in HIV patients.

questions.q: A 70-year-old presents with a solitary, firm, flesh-colored nodule on the face that has grown rapidly over 6 weeks, forming a crateriform structure filled with keratin. It is now starting to regress spontaneously. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is characterized by rapid growth (6-8 weeks) forming a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater, followed by spontaneous regression over months. It is considered by many as a well-differentiated SCC and is treated with excision. The rapid growth-then-regression natural history distinguishes it from true SCC.

questions.q: A medical student is performing a skin biopsy for a suspected bullous disorder. The correct site for biopsy to maximize diagnostic yield on Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF) is:
opts: From the center of the bulla
From perilesional skin adjacent to the bulla
questions.exp: For DIF in bullous disorders, biopsy should be taken from perilesional skin (within 1cm of the bulla edge) or from uninvolved skin adjacent to the lesion. The center of the bulla contains degraded immunoreactants and gives false-negative results. Routine H&E histopathology is performed on the lesional (bulla) skin.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male with a long history of psoriasis is started on a biologic agent. After 3 months, he develops fever, malaise, and a chest X-ray showing a pulmonary infiltrate with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Sputum culture reveals Histoplasma capsulatum. Which biologic is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: TNF-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept) cause significant immunosuppression and increase the risk of serious infections including opportunistic infections like histoplasmosis and tuberculosis reactivation. Screening for latent TB and fungal infections is mandatory before starting anti-TNF therapy. IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors have a lower risk of these serious opportunistic infections.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with tinea capitis showing extensive boggy, pustular, inflammatory plaque with broken hair stubs and cervical lymphadenopathy. The type of tinea capitis present is:
questions.exp: Kerion celsi is a severe inflammatory type of tinea capitis presenting as a boggy, painful, pustular, indurated plaque with broken hairs, sinus formation, and regional lymphadenopathy. It is caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to the dermatophyte. Treatment requires systemic antifungals; the boggy mass should NOT be incised and drained as this delays healing.
